prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in it, opening the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: I keep B047 as my preferred single-part configuration, and I hold it with somewhat less margin than in round 1. The prize criterion is a discovery or invention, and here there is a quantitative prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011: a specific magic twist angle at which the moire bands flatten) followed by an experiment (Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators, 2018) that found correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle, in a platform where a single control parameter, the twist angle, can be set and checked by direct structural characterisation. Reproduction by many groups and extension to other moire platforms within a few years is the confirmation a discovery prize needs; the open mechanism of the superconductivity is a question about what the phases are, not whether they exist. The chair asks whether the citation can be worded around the prediction and observed phases alone. I think it can, and the citation I propose says nothing about mechanism. Three names carry the chain cleanly: Bistritzer and MacDonald for the prediction, Jarillo-Herrero for the decisive observation.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against my own position is maturity and the comparison with B012. Round 1 showed that Eriksson, Kroll, Lindroth, Johansson and Pearce all treat the unsettled mechanism and twist-angle disorder as a reason to wait, and I accept that quantitative comparison with theory is limited by sample-to-sample variation. B012 has more than fifteen years of confirmation by transport, ARPES and STM, and seven of eight members ranked it, so a prize for B047 this year is a judgment that a recent discovery is already secure enough while a more settled one is not obviously overtaken. On credit, the experimental papers have first authors (Cao, Fatemi) and parallel moire work elsewhere (Dean and colleagues) that three names cannot honour, and earlier moire band-structure theory exists. A committee that weights settled interpretation and breadth of agreement above everything else should prefer B012.

responses.point: Pearce prefers B012 because its interpretation is stable after fifteen-plus years, argues that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are the clearest decisive-prediction-plus-first-observation trio available, and says B047's physical meaning is still being argued.
responses.response: I agree that B012 is the more mature case and I said so in round 1. Where I differ is on how the attribution comparison comes out. In B012 the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp's experiment actually tested belongs to Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who sit outside the trio, so the experimental credit is not tied to a named theorist; in B047 the prediction (Bistritzer, MacDonald) and the observation (Jarillo-Herrero) are all inside the three names. You are right that the Nobel record often leaves the wider community out, and I do not treat the gap as disqualifying for B012. But it narrows the advantage you claim for it. On interpretation, I would separate the discovery from its explanation: a prize for B012 is also a prize for a classification whose later materials realisations have been imperfect. I would still rate B012 as the safest outcome, and I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Johansson moved to B012 and argues that maturity should be placed ahead of novelty, that experimental credit for B047 is concentrated in one group with Cao and parallel moire work outside the names, and that he would revisit B047 in a few years.
responses.response: The point about waiting is the serious one and I do not think it is answered by counting reproductions. My answer is that the discovery in B047 is not an interpretation that might be overturned: the flat-band prediction and the correlated insulating and superconducting states have been found by independent groups in several moire platforms, and that part will not change whatever the pairing mechanism turns out to be. The risk a committee runs by waiting is different, namely that the credit becomes harder to fix as the field grows. On concentration, I am comfortable naming one experimental laureate because the 2018 pair of papers preceded the confirming work elsewhere, though I accept that Cao and Fatemi go unrecognised, as often happens under a three-person limit. I would ask you what observation in the next few years would move you; if the answer is only more time, that is a reason to ask again next year, not a scientific objection.

responses.point: Eriksson would keep MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero as the cleanest pair and regards Bistritzer as a defensible third, not as equally decisive; he would not oppose B047 as a second-best option.
responses.response: I want to keep Bistritzer, and I think the correct reading is that the 2011 continuum model, in which he is first author, is what turned flat bands at small twist angles from a qualitative suggestion into a quantitative magic angle. Earlier work on twisted bilayers, as I recall it (Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto; Suarez Morell and colleagues), found velocity renormalisation and band flattening at small angles, but I would want that checked against the record, not rely on my memory. If it holds, it argues for careful wording of the citation around the magic angle, not for dropping a name. A two-person prize would credit the prediction to MacDonald alone and misdescribe the origin. I take your point that you would find B047 acceptable but premature, and I do not claim the case is decisive.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that B019 has had two decades of convergent testing, that the 2005 and 2012 prizes cover the comb and single-ion control but not magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and that B047 is better kept for a later year.
responses.response: Your reply to the novelty objection against the lattice clock is persuasive to me: the earlier prizes concern counting optical cycles and controlling single ions, whereas magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms is a distinct idea, so I no longer regard overlap as the main weakness of B019 and I have moved my view of it up slightly. My remaining hesitation is scope, since it is a measurement achievement whose full recognition may come with the redefinition of the second. I would not oppose it, and it remains my second alternative. I do not accept, however, that B047 is a prize for a later year merely because the understanding is incomplete, for the reasons I gave to Johansson.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a prize for the discovery of correlated phases in magic-angle graphene while the superconducting mechanism is unresolved, or insists on a more settled case such as B012.

Whether the pre-2018 moire band-structure literature (twisted-bilayer calculations of 2007 and 2010) changes the credited set or only the wording of the citation; this has not been checked against the record and rests on my recollection.
How to weigh the unrecognised experimental first authors (Cao, Fatemi) and parallel moire work against Jarillo-Herrero's leadership.
Whether B012 should be preferred this year because of broader support, despite its attribution gaps (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, and the 3D topological-insulator contributors) and the 2016 overlap.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B047, B012 or B019, and I have no documented tie to any credited name. I note my Chalmers affiliation and my colleague Goran Johansson, who prefers B012, and my microscopy network, for completeness. Nothing from round 1 changes this disclosure.
